verdict.root_cause: Roughly two minutes before onset, platform-automation set REDIS_ADDR on cartservice to redis-cart:6380 — a non-default port — and, unlike every prior instance of the same automation cycle, this edit was never reverted and was still in effect when checkoutservice began failing [tr_715d2a4a3f17]. With cartservice pointed at an address where its Redis backend does not serve, cart operations fail or stall, and checkoutservice — which calls cart early in PlaceOrder — accepts requests, logs the order-start record, and then produces none of the downstream payment/email/message-write records that were present in the healthy earlier part of the same window [tr_593c894955c5]. checkoutservice itself has no recorded change in the incident window, keeps serving traffic, and emits no error-level line naming a culprit, so the failure enters it from a dependency rather than originating in it [tr_cf3277e888d1, tr_1696857f43cb, tr_593c894955c5]. The failing mechanism is the configuration value itself: the address names a port that is wrong, and that wrongness is what breaks the request path.
verdict.reasoning: Three things line up. (1) Timing: the only unpaired, still-in-effect change anywhere in the dispatched evidence lands at 22:29:53Z, and the checkoutservice error ratio crosses threshold at 22:30:30Z from a flat-zero 83-sample baseline [tr_715d2a4a3f17, tr_1696857f43cb]. (2) Direction: checkoutservice has no in-window change of its own, did not crash, did not lose traffic, and logs no error or dependency name — the classic shape of a caller inheriting a downstream failure, with the order-start record present but the completion records that follow the cart/payment/email steps absent from ~22:30 onward [tr_cf3277e888d1, tr_593c894955c5, tr_de141567f5c4]. (3) Mechanism: a REDIS_ADDR pointing at a non-default port is a value that is itself wrong; nothing about it is a slow dependency or a mis-shipped artifact, and reverting the value is what stops the failure. The competing explanations inside cartservice's own history were explicitly excluded: the hotfix image and the egress-delay traffic-shaping sidecar were both attached and removed by 15:41Z, leaving a 6.5-hour quiet period before the 22:29 edit [tr_715d2a4a3f17]. The intermittency (mean ~6.4%, sd ~0.19, min 0) is consistent with connection retries and partial cart-path usage rather than a total break, and is the main reason confidence is medium rather than high.
open_questions: No dispatch measured cartservice itself — no cart error ratio, latency, or logs — so the causal link from the REDIS_ADDR value to checkout's failures is inferred across unmeasured edges, not observed.
It was never confirmed that redis-cart does not listen on 6380; if it does, the edit is benign and the real trigger is elsewhere.

Why the checkout error ratio is only ~6.4% and bursty rather than near-total: a hard wrong-address would be expected to fail every cart-touching request, so either only some paths hit cart, retries mask most failures, or the mechanism is timeout-driven.
Checkout's stalled log sequence does not name which downstream step it stops at; payment, email and currency were never queried and remain unexcluded.
The checkoutservice change query ran forward 24h from onset and did not cover the hours before 22:32:30, so a pre-onset change on checkoutservice itself is not ruled out [tr_cf3277e888d1].
Whether the automation loop will eventually emit its own revert (as all 24 prior cycles did) or whether the change is genuinely stuck.

alternatives.root_cause: cartservice or its Redis backend became slow rather than unreachable, and checkoutservice failures are timeouts accumulated while waiting on the cart RPC.
alternatives.why_not: The only latency-injection mechanism in the record — the traffic-shaping container on the cart-service namespace — was removed at 15:41Z and nothing re-attached before onset [tr_715d2a4a3f17], and no latency series was ever collected for cart or checkout [tr_1696857f43cb]. The persisting artifact at onset is an address value, which makes the wrong value, not the wait, the named mechanism. If cart-side latency data later shows elevated p99 with successful-but-slow Redis connections, this overtakes the primary.
alternatives.note: Remediation is the same edit either way, which is why this cannot be dismissed outright.

alternatives.root_cause: A different checkoutservice dependency (payment, email, currency or productcatalog) degraded around 22:30 and the cartservice REDIS_ADDR edit is a coincident, harmless automation artifact.
alternatives.why_not: No dispatch examined those services at all, so this rests entirely on the absence of evidence rather than any positive signal; meanwhile the cart edit is unpaired against a 25-entry history in which every comparable edit was reverted, and lands 2 minutes before a change point on a flat-zero baseline [tr_715d2a4a3f17, tr_1696857f43cb]. Coincidence at that interval is possible but is the weaker reading.

proposal.expected_effect: Restoring cartservice's prior environment (dropping REDIS_ADDR=redis-cart:6380 back to the default address that was in effect through the flat-zero baseline) and recreating the container should, within a few minutes: (1) return the checkoutservice error ratio measured by sum by(service_name)(rate(calls_total{service_name="checkoutservice",status_code="STATUS_CODE_ERROR"}[2m]))/sum by(service_name)(rate(calls_total{service_name="checkoutservice"}[2m])) from its ~6.4% bursty level to the zero it held for all 83 baseline samples, and (2) restore the full per-order log sequence in {service="checkout-service"} — order-start followed again by payment, confirmation-email and message-write records, as seen at ~22:02 — instead of the order-start-only shape present from ~22:30 onward. A short spike of checkout/frontend errors during the container recreate is expected and is not a failure of the fix.
proposal.if_wrong: Falsified if, more than ~5 minutes after the recreate, checkoutservice's error ratio is still bursty above zero and its logs still show order-start records with no downstream payment/email/message-write lines. That would mean either redis-cart does in fact serve on 6380 (making the edit benign) or the stall is in an unqueried downstream — payment, currency, email or shipping — none of which were measured. Note also the weakest link in this proposal: cartservice itself was never measured (no cart error ratio, latency or logs), so the causal edge from REDIS_ADDR to checkout's stall is inferred, not observed. A secondary falsifier: platform-automation re-applies REDIS_ADDR=redis-cart:6380 after the revert, in which case the fix is transient and the automation loop, not the config value, is the thing to stop.
proposal.risk: If the diagnosis is wrong, this restarts a healthy cartservice for nothing: the recreate drops its in-process cache and resets live cart connections, briefly adding checkout failures on top of the existing ones. Worse case: if redis-cart genuinely moved to port 6380 and the 22:29 edit was the correct forward fix that simply lost its pairing entry, reverting points cartservice at a port where Redis no longer listens and converts an intermittent ~6.4% failure into a hard cart outage — the log evidence cannot distinguish these because cartservice was never queried. This is reversible: the 6380 value is recorded and can be re-applied. Also, if platform-automation is mid-cycle, a manual revert may race the automation's own revert or be overwritten by it.
proposal.blast_radius: One service is changed, but its callers notice. frontend calls cartservice directly and will see connection resets and cart-page errors for the duration of the recreate; checkoutservice calls cart early in PlaceOrder and will see a corresponding burst of PlaceOrder failures, which propagates to loadgenerator's success rate. The reverted value is a dependency address, so redis-cart sees traffic move from :6380 back to its default port. accountingservice, currencyservice, emailservice, paymentservice, shippingservice, adservice, productcatalogservice and recommendationservice are untouched except insofar as fewer checkout requests reach them during the recreate.

triage_judgement.reasoning: Simultaneous critical alerts on checkout, frontend, and the load generator indicate a user-facing failure path rather than a quiet warning. No open incidents to attribute it to, and the alerts alone don't distinguish a bad deploy from a failing downstream dependency.
